bib.title: Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Understanding Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate

legacy_report:
SOURCE: "Talk Isn't Always Cheap: Understanding Failure Modes in Multi-Agent Debate", Andrea Wynn, Harsh Satija, Gillian K. Hadfield (JHU and Vector Institute). Preprint, arXiv:2509.05396v2, 13 Oct 2025. Page 1 title matches the expected paper.

COVERAGE: All 13 of 13 pages, 44,373 of 44,373 chars. The paper has no appendices. References were skimmed. I read no figure images, only captions.

CLAIMS (ranked)
- claim: Debate often lowers accuracy compared with majority vote over the same agents' initial answers (no exchange). It does so even when stronger models outnumber weaker ones.
  number: On CSQA, all 9 multi-agent rows fall or hold roughly flat. Mistral x3 falls 44.4 to 39.4 (-5.0). Llama x3 falls 63.0 to 58.6 (-4.4). MMLU Mistral x3 falls 33.6 to 24.4 (-9.2). The largest drop is -12.0 on MMLU in one 1-strong/2-weak mix. The largest GSM8K drop is -6.8. The icons are lost in extraction, so I cannot say which mix the -12.0 row is (see PROBLEMS).
  setup: GPT-4o-mini, Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, Mistral-7B-Instruct-v0.2. Datasets are CommonSenseQA, MMLU and GSM8K. T=2 debate rounds, 100 random questions per task, 5 seeds, mean ± standard error. Final answer is the majority vote. Agents see the other agents' previous-round responses.
  quote: "in the case of CommonSenseQA, which was not studied in prior work on multi-agent debate [Du et al., 2023], debate always harms performance." Also: "even when groups include more "strong" models (e.g., GPT) than "weak" ones (e.g., Mistral), the process of debate does not always yield performance gains."
  where: p.5-6, §5.1, Table 1
- claim: Debate does not reliably beat the best single agent. The strongest single agent (GPT-4o-mini) scores about the same as the best group, and mixed groups often score below it.
  number: GPT single agent scores 74.8 (CSQA), 82.6 (MMLU) and 93.2 (GSM8K). Three-GPT debate scores 74.8, 82.2 and 94.4. Llama single agent scores 57.0, 55.6 and 76.4. Mistral single agent scores 41.6, 34.0 and 34.2. These are my inference from Table 1, not stated in the text.
  setup: As above.
  quote: "74.8±1.9 82.6±2.1 93.2±1.8" (GPT single-agent row); "3× 75.6±2.2 74.8±2.1↓0.8 81.4±3.3 82.2±2.7↑0.8 94.0±0.9 94.4±1.5↑0.4"
  where: p.6, Table 1. The single-agent rows are the top three. The row-to-model mapping is inferred from the three-identical-agent rows.
- claim: Debate helps in some mixes, mainly on GSM8K (open-ended math) and when the group includes a weak model with stronger peers.
  number: The diverse group (one GPT, one Llama, one Mistral) gains +5.6 on MMLU and +3.4 on GSM8K but loses -1.2 on CSQA. Mistral x3 gains +2.8 on GSM8K. One 1-strong/2-weak mix gains +4.4 on GSM8K, and another 1-strong/2-weak mix gains +3.8.
  setup: As above.
  quote: "1× , 1× , 1× 66.6±1.9 65.4±2.1↓1.2 57.8±3.1 63.4±2.1↑5.6 86.8±0.9 90.2±1.2↑3.4"
  where: p.6, Table 1
- claim: Group accuracy often declines as debate rounds progress. This is most pronounced on MMLU and CSQA for mixed-capability groups.
  number: none
  setup: Figure 1, six mixed groups plus Diverse, plus 3x of each model. T=2 debate rounds, with the x-axis showing rounds 1-3.
  quote: "in many group configurations, we observe that performance decreases as the debate progresses. This trend appears across datasets, but is especially pronounced in MMLU and CommonSenseQA, where groups with mixed-capability models often suffer from group performance degradation during debate despite having a majority of stronger agents."
  where: p.6, §5.2, Fig 1
- claim: Agents flip from correct to incorrect more often than from incorrect to correct. The flips grow in round 2, which the authors attribute to social pressure.
  number: none (figures only, no numbers in the text)
  setup: Transition breakdown by group mix and task, aggregated over rounds (Fig 2) and per round (Fig 3).
  quote: "most agents with initially incorrect answers do not improve their performance (peach bars), and, of those that do change their answers, there exists a larger shift in agent responses from correct → incorrect answers (red) than incorrect → correct (green)"
  where: p.7-8, §6.1, Fig 2-3
- claim: An agent is most likely to abandon a correct answer when no other agent agrees with it. The likelihood falls as more peers agree. The effect varies by model and dataset.
  number: none (Fig 4 y-axis runs 0 to 30% probability, with no table)
  setup: Correct-to-incorrect flip probability against the number of agreeing peers (0, 1 or 2), averaged over rounds, per model and task.
  quote: "the likelihood of an undesirable answer-flip is highest when the ego agent is isolated – i.e. when no other agents agree with its answer – and decreases as more peers agree." Also: "on GSM8K, the strongest and weakest models (GPT and Mistral) are far less likely to make undesirable answer-flips than the third model (LLaMA)."
  where: p.8, §6.2, Fig 4
- claim: A prompt-level sycophancy fix does not work. Telling agents their payoff is 1 only for a correct answer does not reduce correct-to-incorrect flips, and in many cases increases them.
  number: none
  setup: Correctness-payoff system and debate prompts versus the base prompt, per model and task (Fig 5).
  quote: "adding a payoff for correctness in the model prompt does not significantly reduce the likelihood that LLM agents flip their answers from correct to incorrect, regardless of the number of other agents that agree with them. In fact, we find that in many cases, the number of correct → incorrect transitions actually increases"
  where: p.10, §6.3, Fig 5
- claim: No single cause explains the failures. Model capability, task type and social influence interact.
  number: none
  setup: Cross-figure observation.
  quote: "no single mechanism, such as sycophancy alone, can fully explain debate failures"
  where: p.10, §6.4
- claim: A theoretical prediction does not hold in practice. Estornell and Liu predicted that diversity of model ability should improve debate. The authors report that it often does not.
  number: none
  setup: Contrast with Estornell and Liu [2024]; mixture-of-agents (Wang et al. 2024) is also cited as the contrary assumption.
  quote: "diversity of model abilities should improve overall debate performance; we show empirical evidence that this is often not true in practice."
  where: p.2
- claim: Suggested fixes, which are not tested.
  number: none
  setup: Discussion section.
  quote: "encouraging agents to assess the soundness of others' reasoning, integrating confidence estimates or credibility scores to weight contributions by expertise, and rewarding independent verification of claims."
  where: p.10-11

LIMITS
- The models are small: GPT-4o-mini and two 7-8B open models. There are no frontier or reasoning models.
- Samples are small: 100 questions per task, 5 seeds, T=2 rounds only. Several deltas are within about 2 standard errors. The paper reports no significance tests.
- Only one debate protocol is tested: all-to-all, summarised peer responses, majority vote, no judge, and no role-based or critic setups. Only one anti-sycophancy intervention is tested, the payoff prompt.
- The social-influence and sycophancy sections are correlational. The authors call the evidence "strong preliminary evidence".
- Cost and token comparisons with a single agent are not measured.
- Task coverage is multiple-choice QA plus grade-school math.
- Generalisation to current models is untested. The authors give no scope caveat beyond the three tasks and three models.

BUILDS ON
- Du et al. 2023 (multiagent debate framework and prompts).
- Subramaniam et al. 2025 (multiagent finetuning).
- Estornell and Liu 2024 ("tyranny of the majority").
- Yao et al. 2025 (sycophancy in debate).
- Wang et al. 2024 (Mixture-of-Agents), which is the contrary assumption being challenged.
- Huang et al. 2023 (LLMs cannot self-correct).
- Sharma et al. 2023 (sycophancy).
- Bullock et al. 2015 and Prior et al. 2015 (accuracy incentives, the source of the payoff idea).
- Wang et al. 2022/2023 (self-consistency).
- Agarwal and Khanna 2025 (persuasive falsehoods fooling judges).

CODE: Code repo at https://github.com/TheNormativityLab/talk-aint-cheap/ (p.5). The debate prompt (§4.3, p.5), verbatim: "These are the solutions to the problem from other agents: {AGENT_RESPONSES} Using the reasoning from other agents as additional advice, can you give an updated answer? Explain your reasoning. Examine your solution and that of other agents. Put your answer in the form (X) at the end of your response."

FIGURES
- Fig 1, p.6: accuracy by debate round per group mix, three panels. It shows the decline over rounds directly.
- Fig 2, p.7: stacked bars of correct/incorrect transitions per mix, with correct-to-incorrect larger than incorrect-to-correct.
- Fig 3, p.7: the same transitions split by round, showing round 2 worse.
- Fig 4, p.8: flip probability against the number of agreeing peers.
- Fig 5, p.9: base prompt versus the payoff prompt. It shows the payoff prompt does not help.

PROBLEMS
- The model icons in Table 1's first column were lost in extraction, so every row label shows only "1×", "2×, 1×" and so on. I can map only the three single-agent rows and the three "3×" rows: GPT 74.8/75.6, Llama 57.0/63.0, Mistral 41.6/44.4 (CSQA). I inferred this from the scores, and the paper does not state it in text. The mixed-row compositions, such as which mix has the -12.0 MMLU drop, cannot be recovered from the text. Check them against the PDF page 6 image before citing a specific mix.
- The Fig 1 and Fig 5 legends are partly garbled but legible.
- The paper does not report numbers for Figs 2-5.
- No embedded instructions were found in the PDF.
